---
title: "About this wiki"
---

## Scope

The wiki covers the federal statutes that most shape U.S. national security policy, in five core areas, plus a group of foreign policy laws they connect to:

- War powers and use of force
- Intelligence and surveillance
- Foreign aid, fragility, and sanctions
- Defense organization and arms transfers
- Civilian harm and protection
- Related foreign policy legislation

A further group, constitutional and code foundations, holds what the rest is built on: the Constitution's war and foreign affairs clauses, the founding-era statutes, the laws that created the National Guard, and overview pages for Titles 10, 22, 32, and 50 of the U.S. Code. Each title page lists every statute in the wiki codified in that title.

A few entries are single U.S. Code provisions, such as 10 U.S.C. 127e or the civilian harm sections of recent defense authorizations, where the provision matters more than the act that carried it. The [Title 10 and Title 50](title10-title50.qmd) page explains the divide between military and intelligence authorities.

Apart from the Constitution page, it covers statutes only. Treaties, executive orders, Defense Department instructions, court decisions, and regulations appear where they explain a statute, but they do not have their own pages.

## What changed in version 2

- **Study guide.** An [eleven-unit curriculum](study/index.qmd) with reading paths, key terms, and review questions, plus [flashcards](study/flashcards.qmd), a [timeline](study/timeline.qmd), and a [glossary](study/glossary.qmd).
- **Authority layers.** Every statute is placed in a layer: Constitution, framework statute, specific authorization, or targeted provision, with the U.S. Code titles as the filing system. Statute pages say what each law builds on, and the graph has a layered view.
- **Civilian harm.** A new domain and study unit covering the Foreign Claims Act, the annual civilian casualty report, the civilian casualty policy requirement, the ex gratia payment authority, and the Civilian Protection Center of Excellence.
- **Two member lenses.** [Rep. Jason Crow (CO-06)](members/crow.qmd) and [Rep. Sara Jacobs (CA-51)](members/jacobs.qmd), with a [comparison page](members/index.qmd). Members are now named.
- **Official links.** Every statute links to its enacted text and its current U.S. Code section on GovInfo, the Government Publishing Office's official repository, in place of the unofficial Cornell copy. Bills link to Congress.gov. The [Sources](sources.qmd) page lists everything the wiki draws on.
- **Current law only.** A switch in the top bar hides repealed and superseded laws from lists, tables, and graphs across the site.
- **Graph.** Click a domain to fade the others; click a statute to filter the connections table to it.

[Version 1](v1/index.html), the October to November 2026 edition with one anonymized member lens, is archived unchanged. On the published site it lives under `v1/`; locally it appears after a full render.

## Member lenses

The [member lenses](members/index.qmd) map each member's committee seats, legislative record, and district interests onto the statutes. They are independent references built from public sources, not affiliated with or endorsed by either member's office, and they describe the record without taking a position on it.

## Reading a statute page

Each page has the same parts: a citation bar whose citations link to the official text, the law's status and layer, a short summary, buttons to read the enacted text and current code, key provisions, why the law matters, its current status, where it sits (layer, what it builds on, code title, era, study units, member lenses), its connections to other statutes, and sources.

Links to repealed and superseded statutes are marked with a dagger (†).

## Relationship types

Connections are directional and use a fixed vocabulary.

| Relationship | Meaning |
|---|---|
| amends | The first statute changed the text of the second. |
| repeals | The first statute repealed the second, in whole or in part. |
| succeeds | The first statute took over the role of the second. |
| relies on | The first statute operates through authority or machinery in the second. |
| constrains | The first statute limits how the second may be used. |
| enacted in | The first statute was passed as part of the second, usually a defense authorization. |
| related to | A thematic or historical link without a direct legal dependency. |

The first four count as dependencies: they make up a statute's "builds on" and "built upon by" lists.

## Layers

| Layer | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Constitution | The grants and limits every statute draws on. |
| Framework statute | A standing law that creates an institution or a general procedure other laws plug into. |
| Specific authorization | A law aimed at a particular conflict, country, program, or problem, usually working through a framework statute. |
| Targeted provision | A single section that grants a narrow authority, imposes a condition, or requires a report. |
| U.S. Code title | The subject shelf where enacted law is filed. |

Layer assignments are editorial judgments, not legal categories.

## Status labels

| Status | Meaning |
|---|---|
| In force | The statute is current law. It may have been amended. |
| Partly expired | Core provisions are current, but significant authorities have lapsed or depend on short extensions. |
| Lapsed | The central authority expired and had not been renewed at last review. |
| Repealed | Congress repealed the statute. |
| Superseded | A later statute replaced it. |

## Accuracy and limits

The summaries were drafted with Claude, an AI model, and reviewed on November 10, 2026. Items that changed in 2025 and 2026 were checked against current reporting, and those sources are listed on the relevant pages. The civilian harm entries were checked against the GovInfo text of the U.S. Code, and bill numbers on the member pages were checked against GovInfo bill status records. Other citations and section numbers were written from reference knowledge and have not each been checked against the primary text.

Treat the wiki as a map for finding and relating statutes. Before citing a provision in your own work, confirm it in the official text linked on each page. Statutes with sunset clauses or disputed implementation change fastest; their pages end their status note with "Check current status."

This is a reference tool and not legal advice.

## Adding or changing content

All content lives in `data/`. The pages in `statutes/`, `members/` (apart from `index.qmd` and `_lens.qmd`), and `study/units/` are generated and should not be edited by hand.

1. Add or edit an entry in one of the files in `data/statutes/`. Copy an existing entry to get the fields right, including `layer`.
2. Add rows to `data/edges.csv` for its connections, using the relationship types above.
3. Add the statute to a unit in `data/study/units.yml`.
4. Run `Rscript R/deploy.R`. The build script checks the data and stops with a message if an ID, domain, layer, status, or relationship is not recognized.
